solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Travellers needing permits to go on motorway

blocks.note: the M1 is Britain's first motorway, written MI in crosswords
permits as a verb: allows, grants

explanation.surface: People on the move need permission before they can drive on the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go on' puts the permits after the motorway; in an across clue the second piece follows the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Migrants are people who move from one region or country to another, so they are travellers.

clue.text: One taking steps to demonstrate?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone taking action in order to prove a point
setter's reading: a protester literally walking in a street demonstration

explanation.walkthrough: 'taking steps' sounds like taking measures; it is literal walking, and 'demonstrate' is a political protest.
explanation.definitionFit: A marcher is a protester who walks in a march, a common form of public demonstration.

clue.text: Handed over pounds for something in the auction room

blocks.note: past tense of give
L is the abbreviation for pounds, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A bidder paid money for an item bought at auction.
explanation.definitionFit: A gavel is the small hammer an auctioneer strikes to close each sale.

clue.text: Time remained for work in the morning

indicators.note: the words are put to work, i.e. worked over and rearranged into something new

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone had time left over to get some work done before lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: Ante meridiem is the Latin behind the abbreviation a.m.
explanation.definitionFit: Ante meridiem is Latin for before midday, the phrase that a.m. abbreviates, so it means in the morning.

clue.text: Quaint daughter finds Scottish material

blocks.note: twee is a British word for quaint or over-cute
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A girl with old-fashioned taste comes upon some cloth made in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweed is a rough woollen cloth, named after the River Tweed and associated with Scottish weaving.

clue.text: Ruler appearing in The Mirror

indicators.note: something appearing in the following words is sitting inside them, waiting to be read out

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A monarch shows up in a tabloid newspaper, the Mirror.
explanation.definitionFit: An emir is a Muslim prince or commander, a title for the ruler of a Gulf state.

clue.text: Saint helping beggar with one drink

blocks.note: St Martin of Tours famously cut his cloak in half to share it with a beggar
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A charitable saint gives a beggar a single drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A martini is a cocktail of gin or vodka with vermouth, a well-known drink.

clue.text: Tear on in small city

blocks.note: a rip is a tear in fabric
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone rushes onward through a little city.
explanation.walkthrough: Ripon is a cathedral city in North Yorkshire, one of England's smallest cities.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripon has city status thanks to its cathedral despite being only a small market town in size.

clue.text: Configurations requiring skills — line up follows to enter

indicators.note: the middle pieces are to enter the first, so they are placed inside it

blocks.note: arts are skills, as in the arts of war
to range is to line up or set in a row
read as followers: a leader's men are those who follow

explanation.surface: Setting things up requires skill: line up the queue, and then those behind come in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'follows' reads as a verb but is taken loosely as a noun, a leader's body of followers; 'line up' is a verb meaning to set in a row, not a noun queue.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrangements are the ways things are set out or organised, i.e. configurations.

clue.text: Fixture I have to join front and back of raiment

indicators.note: the contraction is made to join two letters by going between them
only the first and last letters of the following word are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters of raiment
the contraction I've, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone sewing a fastener onto both ends of their clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Raiment is an old word for clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A rivet is a metal pin that holds plates together, a kind of fastening or fixture.

clue.text: Fancy drape or pendant

indicators.note: fancy as a verb or adjective suggests something elaborated or dressed up, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Comparing an ornate curtain with a hanging decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: An eardrop is an earring with a hanging ornament, i.e. a pendant worn on the ear.

clue.text: Henry appearing in Greenwich a lot

indicators.note: a name appearing in the next words is lodged inside them as a run of letters

blocks.note: letters spanning the end of Greenwich and the next two words

explanation.surface: King Henry, born at Greenwich, was often seen there.
explanation.walkthrough: Hal is the familiar form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hal is a traditional nickname for anyone called Henry, most famously the young Henry V.

clue.text: I dominate after ruining diplomacy

indicators.note: the words are read once they have been wrecked, so their letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bully boasts of taking charge once negotiations have collapsed.
explanation.definitionFit: Mediation is intervention to settle a dispute, a form of diplomacy between parties.

clue.text: Engineers go and come back again

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps
a go is a turn, as in a game

explanation.surface: Engineers come and go on a site visit, then come back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go and come' looks like one phrase; 'go' is the noun meaning a turn, and 'and' joins it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To return is to arrive back where one was before, i.e. come back again.

clue.text: Cockney criminal that has gone to pot

blocks.note: first meaning: rhyming slang for thief
second meaning: what is put into a teapot when brewing

explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang swaps a word for a phrase that rhymes with it. 'Gone to pot' means ruined, but here it is literal: put into the teapot.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea leaf rhymes with thief in Cockney slang, and tea leaves literally go into the pot when making tea.

clue.text: What's discriminating against oldies? Some umbrage is taken

indicators.note: only some of the following letters are used, a consecutive stretch within them

blocks.note: letters across the three words

explanation.surface: Elderly people get offended when they meet prejudice against them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ageist describes prejudice on grounds of age, typically unfair treatment of older people.

clue.text: Model building for worship with roof of timber

indicators.note: in a down clue the roof is the top, so the first letter of the next word is kept

blocks.note: a temple is a place of worship
the top letter of timber

explanation.surface: A church built with a wooden roof serves as a pattern for others.
explanation.definitionFit: A templet is a variant spelling of template, a pattern or model used as a guide.

clue.text: Firm's office cleaner crosses road excitedly

indicators.note: acting excitedly means moving about wildly, so these letters are scrambled
a thing that crosses something stretches over it, so it goes around the other piece

blocks.note: a broom is a tool for cleaning
the letters of road rearranged

explanation.surface: An office cleaner rushes eagerly across the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cleaner' suggests a person; here it is the sweeping implement.
explanation.definitionFit: A boardroom is the room where a company's directors meet, a firm's chief office.

clue.text: County next to Oxon making money

blocks.note: first meaning: short for Buckinghamshire, which borders Oxfordshire
second meaning: US slang for dollars

explanation.walkthrough: Oxon is the abbreviation for Oxfordshire; its eastern neighbour Buckinghamshire is often shortened to the same word as slang for dollars.
explanation.definitionFit: Bucks is the standard short name for Buckinghamshire and also slang for dollars, hence money.

clue.text: Way, beginning to end, to find part of target

indicators.note: the opening letter is taken from the beginning and moved to the end of the word

blocks.note: a route is a way

explanation.surface: Instructions for moving across from start to finish to reach part of a target.
explanation.walkthrough: The outer is the outermost ring of an archery or darts target.
explanation.definitionFit: On a target the outer is the ring furthest from the bull, so it is one part of it.

clue.text: Tot not everyone heard

indicators.note: heard means we go by how the phrase is pronounced, not how it is written

blocks.note: not everyone, only some of them

explanation.surface: A small child that not all people could hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' looks like a small child; it is the verb or noun for adding up, as in tot up.
explanation.definitionFit: A tot is an addition sum, as in tot up, meaning a total or calculation.

clue.text: Fur that is black appearing in trade event

indicators.note: a letter appearing in a word is placed inside it

blocks.note: a sale is an event for trading goods
B is the pencil abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: Dark fur is on offer at a market or sale.
explanation.walkthrough: Sable is itself a word for black, so 'Fur that is black' reads nicely as a whole, though only 'Fur' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sable is the prized dark pelt of a small Siberian marten, a luxury fur.

clue.text: Merciful opponent of Winston?

blocks.note: first meaning: lenient, showing mercy
second meaning: the first name of Attlee, Labour leader who beat Churchill in 1945

explanation.walkthrough: Clement Attlee led Labour against Winston Churchill and won the 1945 general election; the question mark flags the indirect clue to a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement as an adjective means mild or forgiving, and it was also the first name of Churchill's rival Attlee.

clue.text: Chemist and bishop participating in winter festival

indicators.note: someone participating in an event is inside it, so one letter goes within the other word

blocks.note: Noel is Christmas
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A scientist and a cleric join in the Christmas celebrations.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Nobel was the Swedish chemist who invented dynamite and founded the Nobel Prizes.

clue.text: Son frequently delicate

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son
oft is a poetic word for often

explanation.surface: A boy who is often fragile or sickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft and delicate are synonyms for something gentle or easily damaged.

clue.text: The female's laid into unruly child being most impudent

indicators.note: laid into means put inside something, so one piece is set within the other

blocks.note: a brat is a badly behaved child
the contraction she's, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A mother lays into her cheeky child for bad behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laid into' suggests scolding; here it means placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Brashest is the superlative of brash, meaning bold and self-assertive to the point of rudeness.
